reportText:
The patient described distress related to a prolonged and highly conflictual divorce, separation from children, and the emotional impact of allegations he says were false. He reported past suicidal thoughts at the start of the crisis but stated he is not the suicidal type and has since experienced extensive healing. He identified ongoing needs around pornography relapse prevention, sexual boundaries, emotional regulation, accountability, parenting/reintegration with children, communication and conflict management, self-esteem, and trust.

In this text intake, the patient described being in the middle of an extremely messy divorce and stated that his ex-partner falsely accused him of abuse, molestation, and other serious allegations. He reported that two psychological forensic investigations, a police forensic investigation, and a social worker forensic investigation with the children all confirmed his innocence, as he understands it. He said the situation left him broken and traumatized at first, and that in the beginning he did not want to live anymore, though he clarified that he is not the suicidal type and would have welcomed death rather than actively intending suicide. He reported extensive healing since then, but still misses his family and continues fighting to see his children after about one and a half years. He said the children are in therapy to prepare for reintegration.

He then listed the areas where he believes he still needs help. These included pornography relapse prevention; healthy sexual boundaries after past experimentation in the marriage, including a third partner; emotional regulation for stress, sorrow, anger, rejection, and loneliness; insight and accountability regarding his actions and relationship dynamics; guidance for rebuilding child-focused contact and parental capacity; communication and conflict management for future co-parenting; self-esteem, social withdrawal, dependency, and trust; and reintegration therapy for when he sees his children again. He stated that he has already made progress in several areas, but that sorrow, loneliness, self-esteem, and trust remain difficult at times. He also said he discusses these issues regularly with his mother, and that he has been helped by Mr Louw Alberts and God in overcoming pornography. He expressed regret and self-blame about what happened in the marriage, and said he wants to avoid causing further pain or trauma to the children.

The intake centers on divorce-related trauma, separation from children, and the patient’s wish to address pornography relapse prevention, sexual boundaries, emotional regulation, accountability, parenting, communication, self-esteem, and trust. He described a past passive wish to die at the start of the crisis but reported substantial healing and no active suicidal intent in the text. Follow-up should clarify current safety, current coping, and concrete reintegration needs.

Patient presents with a highly structured, self-reflective account of distress tied to marital breakdown and child separation. He repeatedly emphasizes responsibility, regret, and the desire to repair harm without vilifying the other parent. The most clinically salient issues are historical passive death wish, shame/self-criticism, trust disruption, and the need for practical reintegration/co-parenting guidance. Supportive factors include motivation, mother involvement, spiritual coping, and reported progress with pornography control.

sections.title: 3. Key Observations
bullets: Acute relational trauma and grief - The divorce and separation from children appear to be the central stressor, with ongoing grief, loss, and emotional injury. - Evidence: "extremely messy divorce"; "broken and traumetized"; "still miss my family sometimes"

Passive death wish during initial crisis - He described a period of wishing for death rather than active suicidal intent, which warrants follow-up for current safety and mood. - Evidence: "in the beginning I didn't want to live anymore"; "I am not the suicidal type, but I would have welcomed the end with a smile"

Moral injury and self-blame - He repeatedly framed himself as responsible for marital harm and expressed shame and self-reproach. - Evidence: "I know the things I allowed in our marriage was my fault"; "I sometimes even get to the point where I hate myself for what I allowed"

Relapse prevention and behavioral control - Pornography is described as a past vulnerability that he wants to keep under control. - Evidence: "The pornography, just to make sure I do not have a relapse"

Parent-child reintegration anxiety - He is motivated to reconnect with the children but is worried about how to speak to them without increasing harm. - Evidence: "This is the one thing I am the most excited about, but also scared of"; "How and what do I say to them"
Trust disruption - He reported difficulty imagining trusting others after the relationship rupture. - Evidence: "I am having issues even imagining trusting people again"

Co-parenting and communication strain - He anticipates future co-parenting and wants help avoiding escalation and communicating in a child-focused way. - Evidence: "especially because we will need to co-parent"

The narrative is organized, detailed, and goal-directed. - He appears able to identify specific treatment targets and articulate what he wants help with. - Evidence: The message lists eight numbered areas of support and ends with "These are the most important points in short."

He shows ambivalence between anger and compassion toward the ex-partner. - This may be relevant for co-parenting work and emotional regulation. - Evidence: "I do not hate her, I am not even always angry at her. I feel sorry for her"

He reports ongoing shame and self-criticism. - This may contribute to low self-esteem, depressive symptoms, and difficulty with boundaries. - Evidence: "I sometimes even get to the point where I hate myself for what I allowed"

He describes some recovery and resilience. - There are existing coping resources that may support treatment engagement. - Evidence: "I have gone through extensive healing since then" and "I was able to grow stronger"

He identifies support figures and spiritual coping. - These may function as protective supports if they remain stable and appropriate. - Evidence: "with the help of Mr Louw Alberts and God" and "I discuss this with my mother on a regular basis"
Risk level: Low to moderate, based on self-reported historical passive death wish and current distress; no active suicidal intent was stated in the transcript.

He reported that at the start of the divorce crisis he did not want to live anymore and would have welcomed death, but he also stated that he is not the suicidal type and described extensive healing since then. No current plan, intent, or self-harm behavior was reported in the transcript. Ongoing stressors include divorce conflict, separation from children, shame, loneliness, and trust difficulties.

Motivation for treatment - He explicitly requested help in multiple areas and appears engaged in change-oriented work.
Support from mother - He reports regular discussion with his mother, which may provide emotional containment and accountability.
Spiritual support - He identified God as part of his recovery from pornography and distress.
Insight into behavior - He shows awareness of his own role, boundaries, and areas needing growth.
Commitment to children - His desire to reconnect in a safe, age-appropriate way may support sustained engagement and restraint.
Reported progress since crisis - He described extensive healing and improved resistance to pornography.
